question.text: Let $C$ be the intersection of the paraboloid $z=10-x^2-y^2$ and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes $x+y=1,$ $x=0,$ and $y=0.$ Given that the curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above and $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} = \langle -2z, \: 0, \: 0 \rangle,$ the circulation of $\mathbf{F}$ along $C$ can be written as \[ \displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}} = \]
question.explanation:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

\[ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z=10-x^2-y^2$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation

\[ z = g(x,y) = 10-x^2-y^2. \]

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(10-x^2-y^2) = -2x \\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(10-x^2-y^2) = -2y \end{align*}

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

\begin{align} \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \, \Big|_{z=g(x,y)} &= \langle -2z, \: 0, \: 0 \rangle \Big|_{z=10-x^2-y^2} \\[5pt] &= \big\langle -2(10-x^2-y^2), \: 0, \: 0 \big\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle \underbrace{2x^2+2y^2-20}_{P}, \: \underbrace{0}_{Q}, \: \underbrace{0}_R \big\rangle \end{align}

So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \big( -(2x^2+2y^2-20) \cdot (-2x) - 0 \cdot (-2y) + 0 \big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D (4x^3+4xy^2-40x) \: \textrm{d}A, \end{align*}

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_D (4x^3+4xy^2-40x) \: \textrm{d}A &= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1-x}} \,\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}4x^3+4xy^2-40x} \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t) = (2t^3-2t)\,\mathbf{i} + (t+t^2) \, \mathbf{j} + (-t-t^2)\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [-1,0).$ Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=y\,\mathbf{i}+x\,\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral \[ \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]
question.explanation:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

\[ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 2t^3-2t, \qquad y = t+t^2, \qquad z = -t-t^2. \]

So,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) &= y\,\mathbf{i}+x\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= (t+t^2)\,\mathbf{i}+(2t^3-2t)\,\mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(2t^3-2t)\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t+t^2)\,\mathbf{j} - \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(-t-t^2)\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= (6t^2-2) \, \mathbf{i} + (1+2t) \, \mathbf{j} + (-1-2t) \, \mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r' (t) &= \left((t+t^2)\,\mathbf{i}+(2t^3-2t) \,\mathbf{k} \right) \cdot \left( (6t^2-2) \, \mathbf{i} + (1+2t) \, \mathbf{j} + (-1-2t) \, \mathbf{k} \right) \\[5pt] &= (t+t^2) \cdot (6t^2-2) + 0 \cdot (1+2t) + (2t^3-2t) \cdot (-1-2t) \\[5pt] &= 2t^4+4t^3+2t^2 \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{0} \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{0} ( 2t^4+4t^3+2t^2) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \left[\dfrac{2t^5}{5}+ t^4 + \dfrac{2t^3}{3} \right]_{-1}^{0} \\[5pt] &=0-\left(-\dfrac{2}{5}+1-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{15} \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

\[ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z=1+x^2+2y^2$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation

\[ z = g(x,y) = 1+x^2+2y^2. \]

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(1+x^2+2y^2) = 2x \\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(1+x^2+2y^2) = 4y \end{align*}

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

\begin{align} \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \, \Big|_{z=g(x,y)} &= \langle y, \: -x, \: 1 \rangle \Big|_{z=1+x^2+2y^2} \\[5pt] &= \big\langle y, \: -x, \: 1 \big\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle \underbrace{y}_{P}, \: \underbrace{-x}_{Q}, \: \underbrace{1}_R \big\rangle \end{align}

So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \big( -y \cdot (2x) - (-x) \cdot (4y) + 1 \big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D (2xy + 1) \: \textrm{d}A, \end{align*}

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_D (2xy + 1) \: \textrm{d}A &= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}x-1}}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0}} \,\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2xy + 1} \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

question.text: Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate \[ \displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}, \] where $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} = \langle -xe^z, \: 0, \: e^z \rangle,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the paraboloid $z=x^2+y^2$ and the plane $z=4.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.
question.explanation:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

\[ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z=x^2+y^2$ and the plane $z=4.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation

\[ z = g(x,y) = 4. \]

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(4) = 0 \\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(4) = 0 \end{align*}

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

\begin{align} \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \, \Big|_{z=g(x,y)} &= \langle -xe^z, \: 0, \: e^z \rangle \Big|_{z=4} \\[5pt] &= \big\langle \underbrace{-xe^4}_{P}, \: \underbrace{0}_{Q}, \: \underbrace{e^4}_R \big\rangle \end{align}

So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \big( -0 \cdot (-xe^4) - 0 \cdot 0 + e^4 \big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D e^4 \: \textrm{d}A, \end{align*}

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle $x^2+y^2=4$ with radius $2$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

\[ x = r \cos\theta, \qquad y = r \sin\theta, \qquad \textrm{d}A = r \, \textrm{d}r \textrm{d}\theta, \]

we obtain

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_D e^4 \: \textrm{d}A &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{2} e^4 \cdot r \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= e^4 \int_{0}^{2\pi} \, \textrm{d}\theta \cdot \int_{0}^{2} r \, \textrm{d}r \\[5pt] &= e^4 \big[ \theta \big]_{\theta=0}^{\theta=2\pi} \cdot \left[ \dfrac{r^2}2 \right]_{r=0}^{r=2} \\[5pt] &= e^4 (2\pi-0) \cdot (2-0) \\[5pt] &= 4\pi e^4. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t) = (t^2-t)\,\mathbf{i} + (t^2-t^3) \, \mathbf{j} + (t^2-t)\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [0,1).$ Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = 2z\,\mathbf{i} + 3y\,\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral \[ \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]
question.explanation:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that \[ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = t^2-t, \qquad y = t^2-t^3, \qquad z = t^2-t. \]

So, \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & = 2z\,\mathbf{i} + 3y\,\mathbf{k}\\[5pt] & = (2t^2 - 2t)\,\mathbf{i} + (3t^2-3t^3)\,\mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get \begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) & = \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t^2-t)\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t^2-t^3)\,\mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t^2-t)\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] & = (2t-1) \, \mathbf{i} + (2t-3t^2) \, \mathbf{j} + (2t-1) \, \mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r' (t) & = \left( (2t^2 - 2t)\,\mathbf{i} + (3t^2-3t^3)\,\mathbf{k} \right) \cdot \left( (2t-1) \, \mathbf{i} + (2t-3t^2) \, \mathbf{j} + (2t-1) \, \mathbf{k} \right) \\[5pt] & = (2t^2 - 2t)\cdot(2t-1) + 0\cdot (2t-3t^2) + (3t^2-3t^3)\cdot(2t-1) \\[5pt] & = (-3t^3+5t^2-2t)\cdot(2t-1) \\[5pt] & = 2t - 9t^2 + 13t^3 - 6t^4. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \left(2t - 9t^2 + 13t^3 - 6t^4\right) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \left[ t^2 - 3t^3 + \dfrac{13}{4}t^4 - \dfrac{6}{5}t^5 \right]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= 1 - 3 + \dfrac{13}{4} - \dfrac{6}{5} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{20} \end{align*}
